b: There has to be something thrilling as a comedic actor about being tapped by Michael Schur, the creator of “Parks and Recreation,” “The Good Place,” and “A Man on the Inside,” among others. He’s quite simply one of the best comedy writers in television history, and he’s made stars out of so many people by giving them the witty writing needed to showcase their perfect timing. His latest, co-created with star Amy Poehler from the book Excavations by Kate Myers, is the Peacock original “Dig,” a pleasant holiday diversion that only feels minor because of the major shows its creator has unearthed in the past.

In fact, one can pick out character types from previous Schur projects—the five leads almost exactly parallel those from “The Good Place”—but to say that something reminds one of some of the best comedies of the last 20 years is only a minor complaint in the current dire landscape of television that intends to make you laugh.

Poehler plays Elise, the head of an educational excavation site in Greece; she’s as driven as Leslie Knope of “Parks,” but with more hard-earned bitterness about a thankless job that usually produces nothing but dirt. Her boss, Neville (Hugh Laurie), is one of those guys who’s constantly talking about ceding complete control of the site to Elise, but she’s not exactly the kind of people person who’s easy to follow.

Laurie delivers one of the funniest performances in a turn that pokes fun at British superiority, no more so than in a hysterical episode in which he finds a bingo card the students use to play with his consistent personality quirks. It’s a reminder of how funny Laurie can be with the right acerbic material, echoing his wit from “House.”
DIG — Pictured: (l-r) Brennan Lee Mulligan as Marcus, Amy Poehler as Elise, Hugh Laurie as Neville — (Photo by: Colleen Hayes/Peacock)

“Dig” is not a Hugh Laurie show. On the contrary, it centers four very different personality types, led by the arguably uptight Elise. She’s reunited with an old ally named Dylan (Geraldine Viswanathan), who fled the dig site five years ago, leaving heartbreak in her wake. The site’s head preservationist is the upper-crust Brit Clare (Antonia Thomas), who brings mommy issues with her, along with a possible love triangle involving Dylan and Clare’s fiancée.

Finally, there’s the show-stealing Fina Strazza as Patty (not short for Patricia, but long for Pat), a 20-year-old undergrad assistant who is one of those delightfully innocent, quirky characters from the Schur-verse, like Andy Dwyer and Jason Mendoza. She is consistently the funniest thing a show has, and she would be a star if such a thing were possible from Peacock originals in 2026.

One can play a game drawing lines from this quartet (plus a graying older actor on the edge) to the cast of “The Good Place”: Pat is Jason, Elise is Chidi, Dylan is Eleanor, and Clare is Tahani. Simple but true. However, “Dig” is nowhere near as thematically ambitious as one of the best comedies of its era. It’s not even as emotionally rich as “Man on the Inside,” a show that was increasingly dense with ideas about grief and self-discovery. Naturally, there’s some of that in a show set at a dig site, but this comedy is surprisingly surface-level for a creator so endlessly interested in the human condition that he wrote a book called How to Be Perfect.
DIG — Pictured: (l-r) Fina Strazza as Patty, Antonia Thomas as Clare, Amy Poehler as Elise, Geraldine Viswanathan as Dylan — (Photo by: Colleen Hayes/Peacock)

If “Dig” is just a diversion for Schur and his fans, then it’s an entertaining one. As is often the case with his shows, there are no weak links in the ensemble, and there are fun supporting turns from familiar faces as well, including Jason Mantzoukas, Brennan Lee Mulligan, and, most of all, Kayvan Novak as the mayor of the town around the dig site, and a love interest for Elise. The “What We Do in the Shadows” star does his best work since that FX hit, and it’s great to see him again.

There’s a “great to see them” vibe to all ten episodes of “Dig.” It’s a hangout show that’s at its best away from its plot—the story hinges on a discovery by the quartet that could change the history books forever and a mystery involving its sudden disappearance, but it’s more fun just watching Viswanathan and Strazza chase sheep off a Greek road.

As with many Schur programs, it’s about taking four very different personalities and bouncing them off each other in unexpected, smart ways. Schur and Poehler love to dissect how common goals (like local government on “Parks”) can bring together exceedingly different types of people. If this one feels like one we’ve met before, it’s still nice to spend some time with them.
Whole season screened for review. Premieres on Peacock on November 23, 2026.
